## 10. Countries with sustained growth supported by public budgets

*Which countries combined rapid spending growth with sustained fiscal support for health?*

Illustrative cases are selected through common criteria rather than subjective country rankings. Eligible countries must be in the upper quartile of spending growth within their income group, derive at least half of their growth from the combined contributions of government size and health priority, record growth in both halves of the observation window, and have no identified data-quality flag. The results report the underlying growth rates and component contributions for each selected country.

These cases highlight spending trajectories that merit further investigation, particularly where growth has been sustained rather than concentrated in a single interval. They should not be interpreted as evidence of effective policy by themselves. Differences in baseline expenditure and the specific fiscal decisions behind these patterns require additional examination of national budget and policy records.

```{r slide-10-examples, results = "asis", fig.height = 6.4}
## Slide 10: the instructive examples (thresholds by income group, the three
## parts, the total and the two halves).
win <- mine$win |>
  filter(!is.na(total)) |>
  left_join(short_names, by = "iso3")

# the 75th percentile of total growth in each income group, and the examples it gives
thresholds <- win |>
  group_by(income_group) |>
  summarise(
    threshold = quantile(total, 0.75, names = FALSE),
    examples = sum(example %in% TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(match(income_group, INC))
examples <- win |>
  filter(example %in% TRUE) |>
  arrange(match(income_group, INC), desc(total))

# The two halves of each window, such as "2013-18 / 2018-23". We print the most common pair once, in
# the third table, and any other pair after the country's name.
halves <- paste0(
  examples$y0, "-", substr(examples$mid, 3, 4), " / ", examples$mid, "-", substr(examples$y1, 3, 4)
)
halves_in_order <- factor(halves, levels = unique(halves))
halves_count <- table(halves_in_order)
common <- names(which.max(halves_count))
other_halves <- if_else(halves != common, paste0(" (", halves, ")"), "")
example_label <- paste0(examples$short, other_halves)
nepal <- filter(examples, iso3 == "NPL")
nepal_range <- paste(dollars(nepal$ghe0), "to", dollars(nepal$ghe1))

threshold_table <- tibble(
  `Income group` = unname(INC_LABEL),
  `75th percentile of total growth` = one_decimal(thresholds$threshold),
  Examples = thresholds$examples
)
example_table <- tibble(
  `Income group` = unname(INC_LABEL[examples$income_group]),
  Country = example_label,
  Economy = signed(examples$econ),
  `Size of government` = signed(examples$budget),
  `Health priority` = signed(examples$priority),
  Total = signed(examples$total),
  `By half of the window` = paste(signed(examples$half1), "/", signed(examples$half2))
)
also_printed <- tibble(
  Item = c(
    "Examples in all", "Most common half-windows",
    "Nepal, spending per person at the start and end of its window"
  ),
  Value = c(nrow(examples), common, nepal_range)
)
tables <- list(
  "The rule's thresholds and the count of examples by income group" = threshold_table,
  "Instructive examples, log points a year" = example_table,
  "Also printed on the slide" = also_printed
)
show_tables(tables)

# one panel per income group, named without the word "income"
income_panel <- sub(" income", "", INC_LABEL)
bars <- tibble(
  label = example_label,
  econ = examples$econ,
  budget = examples$budget,
  priority = examples$priority,
  total = examples$total,

plot_parts(bars, "label", xlab = "Log points a year", facet = "group") +

## 11. Countries experiencing expenditure declines or erosion of health priority

*Where did government health spending fall, or where did declining health priority offset economic gains?*

Cases warranting closer examination are identified when real government health expenditure per capita declined or when a reduction in health's budget share offset at least half of the positive contribution from economic growth. The offset measure expresses the negative contribution of health priority relative to the positive economic contribution. Countries meeting these criteria but carrying a data-quality flag are reported separately, because sudden breaks, shocks, unusual endpoints, or extreme expenditure levels may affect the estimated trend.

An important finding is that loss of health priority can be obscured by positive overall expenditure growth. Where GDP growth more than compensates for a declining health share, per-capita spending still rises. Assessing fiscal commitment to health therefore requires examining the composition of growth, not only its net direction.

```{r slide-11-warnings, results = "asis", fig.height = 9}
## Slide 11: the warning cases without a data flag (declines and priority offsets), and the
## flagged countries that meet the rule.
win <- mine$win |>
  filter(!is.na(total)) |>
  left_join(short_names, by = "iso3")

# A window other than 2013-2023 goes after the country's name. The offset is the share of the
# economy part that the fall in priority took away.
warn <- win |>
  filter(warning %in% TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    reason = if_else(total < 0, "Decline", "Offset"),
    other_window = if_else(y0 != 2013 | y1 != 2023, paste0(" (", y0, " to ", y1, ")"), ""),
    label = paste0(short, other_window)
  ) |>
  arrange(match(income_group, INC), reason != "Decline", total)
warn_table <- warn |>
  transmute(
    reason,
    Country = label,
    Inc. = unname(INC_CODE[income_group]),
    Economy = signed(econ),
    `Size of government` = signed(budget),
    `Health priority` = signed(priority),
    Total = signed(total),
    Offset = paste0(round(100 * -priority / econ), "%")
  )
declines <- warn_table |>
  filter(reason == "Decline") |>
  select(-reason, -Offset)
offsets <- warn_table |>
  filter(reason == "Offset") |>
  select(-reason)

# the countries that meet the rule but carry a data flag
flagged <- win |>
  filter(warning_rule %in% TRUE, !is.na(flag), nzchar(flag)) |>
  arrange(match(income_group, INC), total)

flagged_table <- tibble(
  `Income group` = unname(INC_LABEL[flagged$income_group]),
  Country = paste0(flagged$short, " (", flagged$flag, ")")
)
counts <- tibble(
  Item = c(
    "Warning cases without a flag", "Declines", "Offsets", "Flagged, listed apart",
    "Lower middle income: declines", "Lower middle income: offsets"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(warn),
    nrow(declines),
    nrow(offsets),
    nrow(flagged),
    sum(warn$reason == "Decline" & warn$income_group == "lower_middle"),
    sum(warn$reason == "Offset" & warn$income_group == "lower_middle")
  )
)
tables <- list(
  "Spending per person fell" = declines,
  "Health priority offset at least half of the economy part" = offsets,
  "Meet the rule but carry a data flag" = flagged_table,
  "Counts on the slide" = counts
)
show_tables(tables)

panel_names <- c(
  Decline = "Spending per person fell",
  Offset = "Health priority offset the economy"
)
bars <- tibble(
  label = warn$label,
  econ = warn$econ,
  budget = warn$budget,
  priority = warn$priority,
  total = warn$total,
  group = factor(panel_names[warn$reason], levels = panel_names)
)
plot_parts(bars, "label", xlab = "Log points a year", facet = "group") +
  labs(title = "The three parts and the total, warning cases without a data flag")
```

## 12. Interpretation and data limitations

*What can and cannot be concluded from an expenditure decomposition?*

Several considerations qualify the interpretation of these results. First, the decomposition is an accounting identity, not a causal model; its components can also move mechanically in opposite directions, as when falling GDP raises government expenditure as a share of GDP. Second, constant-price comparisons depend on price and currency conversions that may be volatile during periods of high inflation or exchange-rate adjustment. Third, changes in statistical classification or accounting practices can create apparent breaks in expenditure shares. GHED's domestic government health expenditure series also excludes certain externally financed resources.

Group medians must be distinguished from aggregates dominated by large member countries. Results can also be sensitive to the endpoints selected and to the operational criteria used to identify examples and cases warranting further scrutiny. The accompanying quality indicators describe the frequency of potential breaks, shocks, extreme endpoints, and unusual expenditure levels; coverage information identifies the countries with incomplete observation windows.

```{r slide-12-limits, results = "asis", fig.height = 3.6}
## Slide 12: data flags by income group and by rule, windows ending in 2024, countries without a
## window, and the largest member of each income group.
win <- mine$win |>
  filter(!is.na(total)) |>
  mutate(any_flag = !is.na(flag) & nzchar(flag))

  group_by(income_group) |>
  summarise(countries = n(), flagged = sum(any_flag)) |>
  arrange(match(income_group, INC))

# the largest member of each income group and its share of the group's spending in 2023
largest <- mine$contrib |>
  filter(income_group %in% INC) |>
  group_by(income_group) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * ghe1_musd / sum(ghe1_musd)) |>

  arrange(match(income_group, INC)) |>
  left_join(short_names, by = "iso3") |>
  transmute(
    `Income group` = unname(INC_LABEL[income_group]),
    `Largest member` = short,
    `Share of the group's spending, 2023` = whole_pct(share)
  )

# windows ending in 2024 and countries without a window, by their full names
names_2024 <- win$name[win$note_2024 %in% TRUE]
names_without_window <- mine$win$name[is.na(mine$win$total)]

flag_table <- tibble(
  `Income group` = unname(INC_LABEL),
  Flagged = flags_by_income$flagged,
  Countries = flags_by_income$countries,
  Share = whole_pct(100 * flags_by_income$flagged / flags_by_income$countries)
)
rule_table <- tibble(

  Rule = c(

# Part II. Fiscal space for government health expenditure, 2027-2029

## 13. Translating fiscal projections into health budget scenarios

*What additional resources could be allocated to health as government budgets evolve?*

The forward-looking framework distinguishes three amounts: the **protect amount**, which maintains health's existing budget share; the **upper ask**, which applies more ambitious but bounded changes in health's share; and the **ceiling**, representing the total projected increase in government expenditure. Together, they provide a transparent starting point for budget discussions, not a substitute for country-specific expenditure planning or a normative spending target.

## 14. Illustrating the framework: Kenya, 2024-2029

*How do macroeconomic projections translate into a potential increase in Kenya's health budget?*

Kenya illustrates the interaction between GDP growth, the projected government-expenditure envelope, and alternative allocations to health. The analysis uses IMF projections of GDP and government expenditure and compares the IMF spending path with a scenario that keeps government expenditure at a constant share of GDP. Values are initially expressed in billions of Kenyan shillings at current prices.

The protect amount preserves the health share assumed for 2026, based on the latest available observation. The ceiling is the increase in total government expenditure above its 2026 level. The upper ask is determined by the largest eligible increase in health's budget share: Kenya's historical trend is positive, but the fixed increase of 0.75 percentage points per year produces the larger eligible amount. Because the 2025-2026 health share is carried forward rather than directly observed, subsequent results should be read as conditional projections, not approved budgets.

```{r slide-14-kenya, results = "asis", fig.height = 6.6}
## Slide 14: Kenya, the method drawn from 2024 to 2029 (GDP, government spending on both paths, the
## health budget at the protect amount and on the upper-ask path), KES billion at current prices.
kenya_lines <- mine$rx_lines |>
  filter(iso3 == "KEN") |>
  arrange(year)
kenya_imf <- filter(kenya_lines, variant == "imf")
kenya_flat <- filter(kenya_lines, variant == "flat")
kenya <- mine$rx |>
  filter(iso3 == "KEN", variant == "imf") |>
  arrange(year) # 2027, 2028 and 2029
kenya_2029 <- filter(kenya, year == 2029)
imf_2029 <- filter(kenya_imf, year == 2029)
flat_2029 <- filter(kenya_flat, year == 2029)

kenya_table <- tibble(
  Item = c(
    "Ceiling, 2026 to 2029", "Health's share of government spending, %", "Protect amount, 2029",
    "Upper ask, 2029", "Upper ask, % of the ceiling", "GDP, 2029",
    "Government spending, 2029, IMF path", "Government spending, 2029, flat share",
    "Health budget at the upper ask, 2029", "Health budget at the protect amount, 2029"
  ),
  Value = c(
    one_decimal(kenya_2029$d_all / 1e9),
    one_decimal(kenya_2029$h),
    one_decimal(kenya_2029$d_protect / 1e9),
    one_decimal(kenya_2029$ask / 1e9),
    whole_pct(kenya_2029$ask_share_of_ceiling_nominal),
    one_decimal(imf_2029$gdp / 1e9),
    one_decimal(imf_2029$gge / 1e9),
    one_decimal(flat_2029$gge / 1e9),
    one_decimal((kenya_2029$health26 + kenya_2029$ask) / 1e9),
    one_decimal(imf_2029$health_protect / 1e9)
  )
)
tables <- list("Kenya, KES billion at current prices, IMF path" = kenya_table)
show_tables(tables)

# Three panels: GDP, government spending on both paths, and the health budget at the
# protect amount and on the upper-ask path
upper_ask <- tibble(
  year = 2026:2029,
  v = c(kenya_2029$health26, kenya$health26 + kenya$ask)
)
flat_from_2026 <- filter(kenya_flat, year >= 2026)
line_names <- c(
  "IMF path", "Flat spending share", "Protect: health's share held",
  "Upper ask: +0.75 points a year"
)
kenya_long <- bind_rows(
  tibble(panel = "A. GDP", year = kenya_imf$year, v = kenya_imf$gdp / 1e9, line = line_names[1]),
  tibble(
    panel = "B. Government spending", year = kenya_imf$year, v = kenya_imf$gge / 1e9,
    line = line_names[1]
  ),
  tibble(
    panel = "B. Government spending", year = flat_from_2026$year, v = flat_from_2026$gge / 1e9,
    line = line_names[2]
  ),
  tibble(
    panel = "C. Health budget", year = kenya_imf$year, v = kenya_imf$health_protect / 1e9,
    line = line_names[3]
  ),
  tibble(
    panel = "C. Health budget", year = upper_ask$year, v = upper_ask$v / 1e9,
    line = line_names[4]
  )
) |>
  mutate(line = factor(line, levels = line_names))
ggplot(kenya_long, aes(year, v, colour = line, linetype = line)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2026, xmax = 2029, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#f2f4f6") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = setNames(c(WB[["blue"]], WB[["grey"]], WB[["rust"]], WB[["navy"]]), line_names)
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = setNames(c("solid", "dotted", "solid", "dashed"), line_names)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2024:2029) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "KES billion, current prices",
    title = "Kenya: the ceiling, the protect amount and the upper ask",
    caption = "Shaded years: IMF projections from 2026."
  )
```

## 15. Fiscal space for health by income group in 2029

*How do the protect amount, upper ask, and fiscal ceiling differ across income levels?*

The comparison reports median country-level increases in 2029 relative to the 2026 baseline under the IMF expenditure path. Estimates are expressed in real terms, both as percentages of the 2026 health budget and as increases in constant-2026 US dollars per capita. Each median is calculated independently; the upper-ask summary includes only countries for which the framework applies.

The ceiling can be much larger than the protect amount when health accounts for only a small share of government expenditure. For example, at a health share of 5%, the ceiling is twenty times the protect amount, compared with roughly seven times at a 15% share. This arithmetic explains why the ceiling may appear very large in percentage terms even where the absolute additional resources available per person remain limited, particularly in low-income countries. It should not be interpreted as an attainable health allocation.

```{r slide-15-groups, results = "asis", fig.height = 4.4}

## income group, in per cent of the 2026 health budget and in constant 2026 US$ per person;

# a dot for each amount on a log scale, joined from the protect amount to the ceiling

  tibble(

## 16. Countries facing a constrained or contracting fiscal envelope

*Where do projected budgets leave no positive nominal fiscal space for the proposed allocation framework?*

The framework requires total nominal government expenditure to exceed its 2026 baseline. When the budget is unchanged or contracting, there is no positive incremental envelope on which to apply the protect and upper-ask rules. The analysis identifies these countries under both expenditure paths and distinguishes nominal expansion from real purchasing-power gains. It also identifies cases where the proposed real upper ask exceeds the real growth of government expenditure.

Under the IMF path, many inapplicable cases reflect a projected reduction in government expenditure relative to GDP rather than a contraction in nominal GDP itself. Holding the government-expenditure share of GDP constant substantially reduces the number of such cases, leaving three countries where nominal GDP is projected to decline. This sensitivity underscores the influence of fiscal-policy assumptions on estimates of prospective resources for health.

```{r slide-16-not-apply, results = "asis", fig.height = 4}

ask_above <- with_projections |>
  filter(variant == "imf", ask_above_real_ceiling %in% TRUE) |>
  distinct(iso3) |>
  nrow()
flat_names <- no_growth$name[no_growth$n_flat > 0]

## 17. What determines the upper-ask scenario?

*How do historical improvements in health priority compare with standard increases in the budget share?*

The upper ask is selected from positive historical trends in health's share of government expenditure and fixed annual increases of 0.25, 0.50, or 0.75 percentage points, provided the resulting amounts remain between the protect amount and the ceiling. The analysis identifies the scenario that sets the upper ask in each year and describes the distribution of historical health-share changes across income groups.

Only one country experienced an annual increase in health's budget share above 0.75 percentage points during its latest observation window. Consequently, the 0.75-percentage-point scenario determines the upper ask for nearly all eligible cases. Although expressed as a uniform absolute change, this assumption represents a substantially larger proportional increase for countries starting from a low health budget share. It is therefore best regarded as an illustrative ambition scenario rather than a universal policy recommendation.

```{r slide-17-setter, results = "asis", fig.height = 3.4}
## Slide 17: which candidate set the upper ask in each year (IMF path), the own trend in health's
## share by band and income group, and the upper ask as a share of the real ceiling.
SETTERS <- c(
  "075" = "+0.75 a year", "050" = "+0.5 a year", "025" = "+0.25 a year", trend = "Own trend",
  none = "None admissible"
)
world_imf <- mine$rx_grp |>
  filter(key == "world", variant == "imf") |>
  arrange(year)
groups_2029 <- filter(mine$rx_grp, variant == "imf", year == 2029)

# the own trend in health's share is the same in every year, so one
# year (2027) gives one row per country
rows_2027 <- filter(mine$rx, variant == "imf", year == 2027)
trends <- rows_2027$trend[!is.na(rows_2027$trend)]
trend_rows <- bind_rows(
  mutate(rows_2027, Countries = "World"),
  mutate(rows_2027, Countries = unname(INC_LABEL[income_group]))
)
bands <- trend_rows |>
  filter(!is.na(trend)) |>
  group_by(Countries) |>
  summarise(
    `Fell or flat` = sum(trend <= 0),
    `Up to 0.25` = sum(trend > 0 & trend <= 0.25),
    `0.25 to 0.5` = sum(trend > 0.25 & trend <= 0.5),
    `0.5 to 0.75` = sum(trend > 0.5 & trend <= 0.75),
    `Above 0.75` = sum(trend > 0.75),
    n = n()
  ) |>
  arrange(match(Countries, c("World", INC_LABEL)))

setter_table <- tibble(
  Year = 2027:2029,
  `+0.75 a year` = world_imf$set_075,
  `+0.5 a year` = world_imf$set_050,
  `+0.25 a year` = world_imf$set_025,
  `Own trend` = world_imf$set_trend,
  `None admissible` = world_imf$set_none,
  `Method applies` = world_imf$n_applies
)
also_printed <- tibble(
  Item = c(
    "Median trend, points a year", "Middle half, from", "Middle half, to",
    "Upper ask, % of the real ceiling, 2029: world", "low income", "high income"
  ),
  Value = c(
    signed(median(trends)),
    one_decimal(quantile(trends, 0.25, names = FALSE)),
    signed(quantile(trends, 0.75, names = FALSE)),
    whole_pct(world_imf$med_ask_share_of_ceiling[world_imf$year == 2029]),
    whole_pct(groups_2029$med_ask_share_of_ceiling[groups_2029$key == "low"]),
    whole_pct(groups_2029$med_ask_share_of_ceiling[groups_2029$key == "high"])
  )
)
tables <- list(
  "Candidate that set the upper ask, IMF path (countries where the method applies)" = setter_table,
  "Own trend in health's share, points a year, latest decade" = bands,
  "Also printed on the slide" = also_printed
)
show_tables(tables)

# the count of each candidate in each year, as a share of the countries where the method applies
set_by <- world_imf |>
  select(
    year,
    total = n_applies, `075` = set_075, `050` = set_050, `025` = set_025, trend = set_trend,
    none = set_none
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(year, total), names_to = "setter", values_to = "n") |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = 2029:2027),
    setter = factor(SETTERS[setter], levels = rev(SETTERS)),
    # we write the count on segments of five countries or more
    label = if_else(n >= 5, as.character(n), "")
  )
ggplot(set_by, aes(x = 100 * n / total, y = year, fill = setter)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label, group = setter),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), colour = "white", size = 3.2
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = setNames(
      c(WB[["navy"]], WB[["blue"]], WB[["light"]], WB[["rust"]], "#d5dade"), unname(SETTERS)
    ),
    breaks = unname(SETTERS)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100), labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.03))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Share of countries where the method applies (labels: countries)", y = NULL,
    title = "Candidate that sets the upper ask, IMF path"
  )
```

## 18. Sensitivity to the government-expenditure path

*How much do projected fiscal-policy choices affect the resources potentially available for health?*

Two alternative expenditure paths are compared for 2029. The IMF path incorporates projected changes in government expenditure relative to GDP, including potential fiscal consolidation. The constant-share path holds government expenditure at its 2026 share of GDP and therefore allows expenditure to change with nominal GDP. The country comparison reports real government-expenditure growth under both assumptions, alongside the resulting protect, upper-ask, and ceiling estimates by income group.

The ceiling is particularly sensitive to the overall government-expenditure path because it encompasses the full increase in the public budget. The upper ask is generally less sensitive, since it reflects a selected share of that envelope, but it can still change materially. The assumed fiscal path also determines whether the framework is applicable when nominal expenditure fails to grow. Any estimate of fiscal space for health should therefore be read in the context of the underlying macro-fiscal scenario.

```{r slide-18-paths, results = "asis", fig.height = 5.6}
## Slide 18: the IMF path against a flat spending share in 2029: country by country real growth of
## government spending, the ceiling and the upper ask on each path, and the medians by income group.
with_data <- unique(mine$rx$iso3[mine$rx$has_data %in% TRUE])
imf_2029 <- mine$rx |>
  filter(variant == "imf", year == 2029, iso3 %in% with_data) |>
  select(
    iso3,
    imf_ceiling = d_all_pct, imf_ask = ask_pct, imf_real = d_all_real, imf_gge26 = gge26
  )
flat_2029 <- mine$rx |>
  filter(variant == "flat", year == 2029, iso3 %in% with_data) |>
  select(
    iso3,
    flat_ceiling = d_all_pct, flat_ask = ask_pct, flat_real = d_all_real, flat_gge26 = gge26
  )

# Each country on both paths. The deck rounds the real growth of government spending to one decimal
# before it places a country on the chart, so we do the same.
paths <- inner_join(imf_2029, flat_2029, by = "iso3") |>
  mutate(
    ask_close = !is.na(imf_ask) & !is.na(flat_ask) & abs(flat_ask - imf_ask) < 5,
    imf_growth = round(100 * imf_real / imf_gge26, 1),
    flat_growth = round(100 * flat_real / flat_gge26, 1),
    in_view = imf_growth >= -50 & imf_growth <= 100 & flat_growth >= -50 & flat_growth <= 100
  )

# the medians by group on each path
imf_groups <- mine$rx_grp |>
  filter(variant == "imf", year == 2029, key %in% c("world", INC)) |>
  arrange(match(key, c("world", INC)))
flat_groups <- mine$rx_grp |>
  filter(variant == "flat", year == 2029, key %in% c("world", INC)) |>
  arrange(match(key, c("world", INC)))

country_counts <- tibble(
  Item = c(
    "Flat share gives a larger ceiling", "Countries",
    "Median difference in the ceiling, points of the 2026 health budget",
    "Upper ask differs by less than 5 points", "Countries outside the chart's view",
    "Does not apply, IMF path", "Does not apply, flat share",
    "Median upper ask per person, IMF path", "Median upper ask per person, flat share"
  ),
  Value = c(
    sum(paths$flat_ceiling > paths$imf_ceiling),
    nrow(paths),
    scales::comma(median(paths$flat_ceiling - paths$imf_ceiling), accuracy = 1),
    sum(paths$ask_close),
    sum(!paths$in_view),
    imf_groups$n_not_applies[1],
    flat_groups$n_not_applies[1],
    dollars(imf_groups$med_ask_usd_pp[1]),
    dollars(flat_groups$med_ask_usd_pp[1])
  )
)
group_medians <- tibble(
  Group = c("World", unname(INC_LABEL)),
  `Ceiling, IMF` = whole_pct(imf_groups$med_d_all_pct),
  `Ceiling, flat` = whole_pct(flat_groups$med_d_all_pct),
  `Ask, IMF` = share_pct(imf_groups$med_ask_pct),
  `Ask, flat` = share_pct(flat_groups$med_ask_pct),
  n = imf_groups$n
)
tables <- list(
  "Countries with IMF projections, 2029" = country_counts,
  "Median real increase, % of the 2026 health budget, 2029" = group_medians
)
show_tables(tables)

in_view <- paths |>
  filter(in_view) |>
  mutate(side = if_else(flat_growth > imf_growth, "Flat share gives more", "IMF path gives more"))
ggplot(in_view, aes(imf_growth, flat_growth)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = WB[["grey"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = WB[["grey"]]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = side), size = 2, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("Flat share gives more" = WB[["blue"]], "IMF path gives more" = "#8f99a3")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(-50, 100), breaks = seq(-50, 100, 25), labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(-50, 100), breaks = seq(-50, 100, 25), labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "IMF path: real growth of government spending, 2026 to 2029", y = "Flat share: real growth",
    title = "Each country, 2026 prices", caption = "Dashed line: the two paths agree."
  )
```

## 19. Country illustrations: Ethiopia, Kenya, and Indonesia in 2029

*How do the proposed scenarios translate into country-specific budget amounts?*

Ethiopia, Kenya, and Indonesia illustrate how the same allocation rules operate under different fiscal and expenditure conditions. For each country, proposed increases are compared with the projected ceiling under the IMF path. Estimates are presented in current national currency, in US dollars using the IMF's 2029 exchange rate, and as real percentage increases relative to the 2026 health budget.

Ethiopia has no eligible historical-trend scenario because health's share declined over its observation window, and projected inflation substantially reduces the real value of nominal increases. Kenya's positive historical trend is smaller than the fixed 0.75-percentage-point scenario. In Indonesia, the upper ask occupies only a limited share of the nominal ceiling. In all three countries, the fixed 0.75-percentage-point increase determines the upper ask, illustrating both the consistency of the rule and the variation in its fiscal implications.

```{r slide-19-examples, results = "asis", fig.height = 4}
## Slide 19: Ethiopia, Kenya and Indonesia in 2029, IMF path: protect amount, candidates, upper ask
## and ceiling, with the share of the real ceiling each represents.
UNIT <- list(
  ETH = list(div = 1e9, cur = "ETB", scale = "billion", name = "Ethiopia"),
  KEN = list(div = 1e9, cur = "KES", scale = "billion", name = "Kenya"),
  IDN = list(div = 1e12, cur = "IDR", scale = "trillion", name = "Indonesia")
)
CAND <- c(
  protect = "d_protect", trend = "c_trend", s025 = "c_025", s050 = "c_050", s075 = "c_075",
  ask = "ask", ceiling = "d_all"
)
CAND_LABEL <- c(
  protect = "Protect", trend = "Own trend", s025 = "+0.25 a year", s050 = "+0.5 a year",
  s075 = "+0.75 a year", ask = "Upper ask", ceiling = "Ceiling"
)

tables <- list()
ladder <- NULL
for (iso in c("ETH", "KEN", "IDN")) {
  row_2029 <- filter(mine$rx, iso3 == iso, variant == "imf", year == 2029)
  unit <- UNIT[[iso]]
  # Each amount in four units: national currency, US$ million, the real rise in % of the 2026 health
  # budget and % of the real ceiling. The own-trend candidate exists only where health's share rose.
  trend_ok <- !is.na(row_2029$trend) && row_2029$trend > 0
  # The builder rounds US$ million to one decimal and the slide prints it whole in
  # JavaScript, which rounds a half away from zero where R's round() goes to the even
  # number; we round in the same two steps.
  amounts <- tibble(
    key = names(CAND),
    nominal = unlist(row_2029[CAND]),
    usd = unlist(row_2029[paste0(CAND, "_usd")]),
    real_pct = unlist(row_2029[paste0(CAND, "_pct")]),
    real = unlist(row_2029[paste0(CAND, "_real")])
  ) |>
    mutate(
      shown = !is.na(nominal) & (key != "trend" | trend_ok),
      of_ceiling = 100 * real / row_2029$d_all_real,
      usd_tenths = round(usd / 1e6, 1),
      # a half away from zero, as in JavaScript
      usd_whole = sign(usd_tenths) * floor(abs(usd_tenths) + 0.5)
    )
  caption <- paste0(
    unit$name, ", 2029, IMF path: health ", one_decimal(row_2029$h), "% of government spending"
  )
  tables[[caption]] <- amounts |>
    transmute(
      Amount = unname(CAND_LABEL[key]),
      `National currency` = if_else(
        shown, paste(unit$cur, one_decimal(nominal / unit$div), unit$scale), "-"
      ),
      `US$ million` = if_else(shown, scales::comma(usd_whole, accuracy = 1), "-"),
      `Real, % of the 2026 health budget` = if_else(
        shown, signed_pct(real_pct), "-"
      ),
      `% of the real ceiling` = if_else(
        shown & !key %in% c("ask", "ceiling"), one_decimal(of_ceiling), "-"
      )
    )
  # the ladder chart: the protect amount and the candidates as % of the real ceiling
  rungs <- amounts |>
    filter(key %in% c("protect", "trend", "s025", "s050", "s075")) |>
    transmute(
      country = unit$name,
      cand = unname(CAND_LABEL[key]),
      v = if_else(shown, of_ceiling, NA),
      role = case_when(
        key == "protect" ~ "Protect",
        key == row_2029$setter ~ "Upper ask",
        .default = "Other candidate"
      )
    )
  ladder <- bind_rows(ladder, rungs)
}
eth <- filter(mine$rx, iso3 == "ETH", variant == "imf", year == 2029)
ken <- filter(mine$rx, iso3 == "KEN", variant == "imf", year == 2029)
idn <- filter(mine$rx, iso3 == "IDN", variant == "imf", year == 2029)
# Ethiopia's price rise as the slide prints it: the builder keeps the price level to three decimals
# and the slide rounds the per cent half up
eth_price_level <- round(eth$p, 3)
eth_price_rise <- floor(100 * (eth_price_level - 1) + 0.5)
setters <- unique(c(eth$setter_label, ken$setter_label, idn$setter_label))
tables[["Also printed on the slide"]] <- tibble(
  Item = c(
    "Ethiopia: own trend, points a year", "Ethiopia: price rise 2026 to 2029",
    "Kenya: own trend, points a year", "Kenya: health's share reached by the ask, 2029",
    "Indonesia: ask, % of the nominal ceiling",
    "Indonesia: health's share reached by the ask, 2029",
    "Upper ask set by, all three"
  ),
  Value = c(
    signed(eth$trend),
    paste0(eth_price_rise, "%"),
    signed(ken$trend),
    share_pct(ken$h_ask),
    whole_pct(idn$ask_share_of_ceiling_nominal),
    share_pct(idn$h_ask),
    paste(setters, collapse = ", ")
  )
)
show_tables(tables)

rung_names <- unname(CAND_LABEL[c("protect", "trend", "s025", "s050", "s075")])
ladder <- ladder |>
  mutate(
    cand = factor(cand, levels = rev(rung_names)),
    country = factor(country, levels = c("Ethiopia", "Kenya", "Indonesia")),
    bar = coalesce(v, 0),
    label = if_else(is.na(v), "share fell: no candidate", one_decimal(v))
  )
ggplot(ladder, aes(x = bar, y = cand, fill = role)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~country) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(Protect = "#8f99a3", "Upper ask" = WB[["navy"]], "Other candidate" = WB[["light"]]),
    breaks = c("Protect", "Other candidate", "Upper ask")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 115), breaks = c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(
    x = "% of the real ceiling (ceiling = 100)", y = NULL,
    title = "Protect amount and candidates, 2029, IMF path"
  )
```

## 20. Annual health budget scenarios for Ethiopia, Kenya, and Indonesia

*What additional spending would each scenario imply in 2027, 2028, and 2029?*

Country-level estimates show how the protect amount, eligible increases in health's budget share, the selected upper ask, and the overall expenditure ceiling evolve from 2027 to 2029 under the IMF path. Each amount represents an increase relative to the 2026 baseline and is reported in current national currency, as a real percentage of the baseline health budget, and in US dollars at the relevant year's projected exchange rate. A missing historical-trend scenario indicates that health's budget share declined during the observation window.

Nominal budget increases should not be equated with increases in purchasing power. The accompanying real percentages adjust for changes in the GDP deflator, allowing the nominal fiscal request to be considered alongside its implied change in real resources. These estimates describe potential budget increments, not expenditure commitments or estimates of health-service delivery costs.

```{r slide-20-policy-table, results = "asis"}
## Slide 20: the policy table for Ethiopia, Kenya and Indonesia, 2027 to
## 2029, IMF path; one table per country.
tables <- list()
for (iso in c("ETH", "KEN", "IDN")) {
  unit <- UNIT[[iso]]
  country_years <- mine$rx |>
    filter(iso3 == iso, variant == "imf") |>
    arrange(year)
  policy_rows <- NULL
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(country_years))) {
    one_year <- country_years[i, ]
    # the amounts as on slide 19: the nominal increase, then (the real rise in %, US$ million)
    trend_ok <- !is.na(one_year$trend) && one_year$trend > 0
    nominal <- unlist(one_year[CAND])
    real_pct <- unlist(one_year[paste0(CAND, "_pct")])
    usd <- unlist(one_year[paste0(CAND, "_usd")])
    shown <- !is.na(nominal) & (names(CAND) != "trend" | trend_ok)
    national <- one_decimal(nominal / unit$div)
    real_rise <- signed_pct(real_pct)
    # US$ million rounded in two steps, as on slide 19
    usd_tenths <- round(usd / 1e6, 1)
    # a half away from zero, as in JavaScript
    usd_whole <- sign(usd_tenths) * floor(abs(usd_tenths) + 0.5)
    usd_million <- scales::comma(usd_whole, accuracy = 1)
    cell <- if_else(shown, paste0(national, " (", real_rise, ", US$", usd_million, " m)"), "-")
    policy_rows <- bind_rows(policy_rows, tibble(
      Year = as.character(one_year$year),
      Protect = cell[1],
      `Own trend` = cell[2],
      `+0.25 a year` = cell[3],
      `+0.5 a year` = cell[4],
      `+0.75 a year` = cell[5],
      `Upper ask` = cell[6],
      `Set by` = sub(" a year", "", one_year$setter_label),
      Ceiling = cell[7]
    ))
  }
  first_year <- country_years[1, ]
  caption <- paste0(
    unit$name, ": ", unit$cur, " ", unit$scale, "; health ", one_decimal(first_year$h),
    "% of government spending; own trend ", signed(first_year$trend), " points a year"
  )
  tables[[caption]] <- policy_rows
}
show_tables(tables)
```

## 21. Implications and limitations for health budget planning

*What additional evidence is needed to turn a fiscal scenario into a credible health budget proposal?*

The framework offers an initial benchmark for discussions about the scale of additional government resources for health. It does not determine whether a proposed allocation is affordable alongside competing priorities, can be executed effectively, or will produce commensurate health benefits. Country-level assessment should therefore consider the latest approved budget, actual expenditure execution, service-delivery capacity, the expected cost and impact of proposed investments, and whether health-sector prices may increase faster than the economy-wide GDP deflator.

Several uncertainties remain. IMF projections are revised periodically, and the historical budget-share trend may mask recent changes in priorities. A government budget can expand in nominal currency while contracting in real terms. Some countries also lack complete IMF series or exchange-rate projections. Regional and income-group comparisons provide context but should not automatically determine country-specific requests. The protect amount and upper ask are planning scenarios, not validated financing needs.

```{r slide-21-limits, results = "asis"}
## Slide 21: coverage of the prescription and the countries without an IMF
## series (the slide is text; no figure).
countries_with_base <- unique(mine$rx$iso3)
countries_with_data <- unique(mine$rx$iso3[mine$rx$has_data %in% TRUE])
world_2029 <- filter(mine$rx_grp, key == "world", variant == "imf", year == 2029)

# The countries without an IMF series, sorted by code point as the deck's builder sorts them, and
# printed without the bracket or the east Jerusalem note in their GHED names
no_imf_names <- mine$rx |>
  filter(!iso3 %in% countries_with_data) |>
  distinct(iso3, name) |>
  arrange(name) |>
  mutate(
    name = sub("\\s*\\(.*\\)$", "", name),
    name = sub(", including east Jerusalem$", "", name)
  ) |>
  pull(name)
no_base_names <- countries$name[!countries$iso3 %in% countries_with_base]

coverage <- tibble(
  Item = c(
    "Countries with a Section 1 base", "Countries with IMF projections",
    "2029 budget grows in currency but falls in real terms, IMF path", "No IMF series",
    "No GHED base"
  ),
  Value = c(
    length(countries_with_base),
    length(countries_with_data),
    world_2029$n_real_fall_only,
    knitr::combine_words(no_imf_names, oxford_comma = FALSE),
    knitr::combine_words(no_base_names, oxford_comma = FALSE)
  )
)
tables <- list("Coverage" = coverage)
show_tables(tables)
```

# Annex A. Country-level decomposition by World Bank region

This annex presents the latest available decomposition for each country, organised by World Bank region. For each country, the tables report the observation window, real government health expenditure per capita in the final year (constant 2023 US dollars), the annualised total change and its three component contributions, and the dominant growth pattern. An asterisk identifies countries where economic growth was positive but health's share of government expenditure declined.

Quality flags indicate a possible **break (B)**, **shock (S)**, **unusual endpoint (E)**, or **extreme expenditure level (L)**. Income groups are abbreviated as **Low**, **LM** (lower-middle income), **UM** (upper-middle income), and **High**. Regional summaries report growth-pattern counts and, where at least eight countries are available, the median change in government health expenditure per capita. The annex provides complete country coverage rather than a ranking of performance.

```{r annex-helpers}
## The seven slides shared by annexes A and B (which countries each
## slide lists), and the annex A table.
annex_slides <- tibble(
  slide = 1:7,
  lead_region = c(
    "East Asia & Pacific", "Europe & Central Asia", "Europe & Central Asia",
    "Latin America & Caribbean", "Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan",
    "Sub-Saharan Africa", "Sub-Saharan Africa"
  ),
  title = c(
    "East Asia and Pacific; South Asia",
    "Europe and Central Asia (1 of 2)",
    "Europe and Central Asia (2 of 2); no World Bank region",
    "Latin America and the Caribbean; North America",
    "Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan",
    "Sub-Saharan Africa (1 of 2)",
    "Sub-Saharan Africa (2 of 2)"
  )
)

# Every country's place in the annexes: regions in the slides' order, countries alphabetical inside
# a region, and the two long regions cut in half over two slides each
region_order <- c(
  "East Asia & Pacific", "South Asia", "Europe & Central Asia", "Not classified",
  "Latin America & Caribbean", "North America",
  "Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan", "Sub-Saharan Africa"
)
annex_countries <- countries |>
  left_join(short_names, by = "iso3") |>
  mutate(
    region = if_else(wb_region == "not_classified", "Not classified", wb_region),
    inc = unname(INC_CODE[income_group])
  ) |>
  arrange(match(region, region_order), sort_name) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  mutate(first_half = row_number() <= ceiling(n() / 2)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    annex_slide = case_when(
      region %in% c("East Asia & Pacific", "South Asia") ~ 1,
      region == "Europe & Central Asia" & first_half ~ 2,
      region %in% c("Europe & Central Asia", "Not classified") ~ 3,
      region %in% c("Latin America & Caribbean", "North America") ~ 4,
      region == "Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan" ~ 5,
      region == "Sub-Saharan Africa" & first_half ~ 6,
      region == "Sub-Saharan Africa" ~ 7
    ),
    annex_position = row_number()
  ) |>
  select(iso3, short, region, inc, annex_slide, annex_position)

# Annex A, one slide: the region line of the slide's lead and the table of every country's latest
# window. We keep this as a function because seven slides use it, each run a second time on the
# report's tables in the final check; `bundle` is `mine` or the report's tables.
annex_a <- function(bundle, slide) {
  this_slide <- annex_slides[annex_slides$slide == slide, ]
  lead_region <- this_slide$lead_region

  # every country on the slide, in the order the slide lists them
  slide_rows <- annex_countries |>
    filter(annex_slide == slide) |>
    left_join(bundle$win, by = "iso3") |>
    arrange(annex_position) |>
    mutate(has_window = !is.na(total))
  table <- slide_rows |>
    transmute(
      Region = unname(REG_LABEL[region]),
      Country = short,
      Inc. = inc,
      `US$` = if_else(has_window, dollars(ghe1, prefix = ""), ""),
      Total = if_else(has_window, signed(total), ""),
      Econ. = if_else(has_window, signed(econ), ""),
      Govt = if_else(has_window, signed(budget), ""),
      Prio. = if_else(has_window, signed(priority), ""),
      Pattern = if_else(
        has_window, paste0(pattern, if_else(lost_priority %in% TRUE, "*", "")), "Not available"
      ),
      Flag = if_else(has_window, coalesce(flag, ""), ""),
      Window = if_else(has_window, paste0(y0, "-", y1), "no constant-price series")
    )

  # the lead: the pattern counts and, for a region with at least eight countries, the median total
  counts <- filter(bundle$pat_reg, key == lead_region)
  latest <- filter(bundle$grp, key == lead_region, period == "W")
  median_text <- ""
  if (grepl("^Carries", latest$status)) {
    median_text <- paste0("; median country ", signed(latest$med_total), " log points a year")
  }
  lead <- paste0(
    REG_LABEL[[lead_region]], ": ", counts$n, " countries, ",
    counts$`Economy-led`, " economy-led, ", counts$`Budget-led`, " budget-led, ",
    counts$`Priority-led`, " priority-led, ", counts$Declining, " declining", median_text
  )

  tables <- list("Lead of the slide" = data.frame(Region = lead))
  tables[[paste0("Annex: ", this_slide$title)]] <- table
  tables
}
```

## 22. East Asia and the Pacific; South Asia

The distribution of real government health expenditure per capita varies widely across the two regions, from low single-digit dollar amounts in some countries to several thousand dollars in Australia and New Zealand. Results for countries with unusual levels or abrupt changes in the published series are accompanied by quality flags and should be interpreted with particular care.

```{r slide-22-annex-a1, results = "asis"}
## Slide 22, annex A1: East Asia and Pacific; South Asia.
tables <- annex_a(mine, slide = 1)
show_tables(tables)
```

## 23. Europe and Central Asia (part 1)

Across Europe and Central Asia, economic growth is the leading contributor to increased government health expenditure per capita in a comparatively large share of countries. The country-level decomposition provides a more detailed view of how the relative contributions of GDP, government size, and health priority differ within the region.

```{r slide-23-annex-a2, results = "asis"}

```

The remaining countries in Europe and Central Asia are followed by the Cook Islands and Niue, which are not assigned to a World Bank region in the classification used here. Their results are retained for completeness without attributing them to a regional aggregate.

```{r slide-24-annex-a3, results = "asis"}

The regional comparison indicates relatively modest aggregate growth in Latin America and the Caribbean, with a limited contribution from economic capacity. Country trajectories are more varied. Venezuela has a shorter eligible observation window because complete data for the three components are available only from 2018.

Several countries, including Afghanistan, Lebanon, Syria, and Yemen, have quality flags indicating potential discontinuities, exceptional shocks, or unusual observations. Their estimated contributions should therefore be assessed alongside the reported data limitations and country context.

Sub-Saharan Africa contains more countries with declining government health expenditure per capita than any other region in the comparison. At the aggregate level, improved budget priority for health contributed more to expenditure growth than economic capacity. Country-level estimates reveal considerable variation around this regional pattern.

# Annex B. Country-level fiscal space scenarios for 2029

The second annex reports the 2029 health budget scenarios for countries with sufficient IMF projections and a usable health expenditure baseline. Estimates under the IMF path include the health budget share carried forward to 2026; the **protect amount**, **upper ask**, and **ceiling** (P, A, and C); and the scenario that determines the upper ask. Changes are expressed in US dollars at the projected 2029 exchange rate and as real percentages of the 2026 health budget.

A country is marked as outside the framework in years when nominal government expenditure does not exceed the 2026 level. **No IMF series** indicates that projections are unavailable. **Not available** in the US-dollar field indicates a missing 2029 exchange-rate projection; real percentage estimates may still be reported. Regional medians summarise the distribution of the protect amount, upper ask, and ceiling where the framework is applicable.

```{r annex-b-helper}
## Annex B: the table of one slide, printing the 2029 prescription row by row.
SET_SHORT <- c(
  "+0.75 a year" = "+0.75", "+0.5 a year" = "+0.5", "+0.25 a year" = "+0.25",
  "Own trend" = "Own trend", "No admissible increase" = "None admissible", "Does not apply" = "-"
)

# Annex B, one slide: the region line of the slide's lead and the table of every
# country's 2029 prescription (IMF path). A function for the same reason as annex_a();
# `bundle` is `mine` or the report's tables.
annex_b <- function(bundle, slide) {
  this_slide <- annex_slides[annex_slides$slide == slide, ]
  imf_path <- filter(bundle$rx, variant == "imf")

  # the years from 2027 to 2029 in which the method does not apply
  years_not_applying <- imf_path |>
    filter(has_data %in% TRUE, !(applies %in% TRUE)) |>
    arrange(year) |>
    group_by(iso3) |>
    summarise(not_apply = paste(year, collapse = ", "))

  # Every country on the slide with its 2029 row. A country without a GHED base (Cuba) has no row
  # and is listed with nothing computed. Amounts are in US$ million, and the real rise in % of the
  # 2026 health budget, for the protect amount, the upper ask and the ceiling (P / A / C).
  slide_rows <- annex_countries |>
    filter(annex_slide == slide) |>
    left_join(filter(imf_path, year == 2029), by = "iso3") |>
    left_join(years_not_applying, by = "iso3") |>
    arrange(annex_position) |>
    mutate(
      has_base = !is.na(variant),
      with_data = has_data %in% TRUE,
      usd_protect = coalesce(dollars(d_protect_usd / 1e6, prefix = ""), "-"),
      usd_ask = coalesce(dollars(ask_usd / 1e6, prefix = ""), "-"),
      usd_ceiling = coalesce(dollars(d_all_usd / 1e6, prefix = ""), "-"),
      pct_protect = coalesce(scales::comma(d_protect_pct, accuracy = 1), "-"),
      pct_ask = coalesce(scales::comma(ask_pct, accuracy = 1), "-"),
      pct_ceiling = coalesce(scales::comma(d_all_pct, accuracy = 1), "-")
    )
  table <- slide_rows |>
    transmute(
      Region = unname(REG_LABEL[region]),
      Country = short,
      Inc. = inc,
      `Share %` = if_else(has_base, one_decimal(h), ""),
      `US$ million P / A / C` = case_when(
        !has_base ~ "No GHED base",
        !with_data ~ "No IMF series",
        is.na(d_protect_usd) ~ "Not available",
        .default = paste(usd_protect, usd_ask, usd_ceiling, sep = " / ")
      ),
      `Real % P / A / C` = if_else(
        with_data, paste(pct_protect, pct_ask, pct_ceiling, sep = " / "), ""
      ),
      `Ask set by` = if_else(with_data, unname(SET_SHORT[setter_label]), ""),
      `Does not apply` = if_else(with_data, coalesce(not_apply, "-"), "")
    )

  # the lead: the region's median protect amount, upper ask and ceiling
  medians <- filter(bundle$rx_grp, key == this_slide$lead_region, variant == "imf", year == 2029)
  lead <- paste0(
    REG_LABEL[[this_slide$lead_region]], ", median of ", medians$n,
    ": protect ", share_pct(medians$med_d_protect_pct),
    ", upper ask ", share_pct(medians$med_ask_pct),
    ", ceiling ", whole_pct(medians$med_d_all_pct), " of the 2026 health budget, real"
  )

  tables <- list("Lead of the slide" = data.frame(Region = lead))
  tables[[paste0("Annex: ", this_slide$title)]] <- table
  tables
}
```

## 29. East Asia and the Pacific; South Asia

South Asia has the largest median ceiling relative to its baseline health budget. This primarily reflects the difference between total projected government-expenditure growth and the comparatively small share of expenditure currently allocated to health. The ceiling should be interpreted as the scale of the overall fiscal envelope, not as an allocation target for the health sector.

```{r slide-29-annex-b1, results = "asis"}
## Slide 29, annex B1: East Asia and Pacific; South Asia.
tables <- annex_b(mine, slide = 1)
show_tables(tables)
```

## 30. Europe and Central Asia (part 1)

Health accounts for a relatively high share of government expenditure in much of Europe and Central Asia. As a result, the projected ceiling is generally a smaller multiple of the protect amount than in regions where health receives a lower initial budget share.

# Reproducibility and validation

The reported results are checked against the reference output tables at the precision used for presentation. The validation compares numerical values (including years and counts) and categorical fields, such as country names and growth-pattern labels. Any discrepancy is identified by its location and stops the rendering process. This provides an explicit check that the analytical tables and the reported results remain consistent.

```{r check-against-report, results = "asis"}
## Final check: every number the slides print, computed in this file, against the same
## number recomputed from the report's output tables (data/reference_outputs.rds).
## Stops with an error on any mismatch.
reference <- readRDS("data/reference_outputs.rds")
stopifnot(all(REF_NAMES %in% names(reference)))
report_tables <- reference[REF_NAMES]
names(report_tables) <- names(REF_NAMES) # the same names as in `mine`

# We read the code of the 34 slide chunks from this file: from the Rmd being knitted, or from the
# file in this folder when the chunks are run one by one in RStudio
rmd_file <- knitr::current_input()
if (is.null(rmd_file)) rmd_file <- "global-decomposition-deck.Rmd"
rmd_lines <- readLines(rmd_file, encoding = "UTF-8")
chunk_starts <- grep("^```\\{r slide-[0-9]+", rmd_lines)
chunk_ends <- grep("^```\\s*$", rmd_lines)
stopifnot(length(chunk_starts) == 34)

# all the cells of a slide's tables, as they are printed, table by table and column by column
cells <- function(tables) {
  printed <- character(0)
  for (table in tables) {
    for (column in table) printed <- c(printed, as.character(column))
  }
  printed
}

# We run each slide chunk twice more, each time in an environment of its own: once on this
# file's tables, and once with `mine` replaced by the report's tables. A run leaves the
# slide's tables in `tables`; capture.output() drops what the run prints, and invisible()
# keeps its figure from being drawn again.
result <- NULL
details <- list()
for (start in chunk_starts) {
  slide_id <- sub("^```\\{r (slide-[0-9]+).*$", "\\1", rmd_lines[start])
  end <- min(chunk_ends[chunk_ends > start])
  slide_code <- parse(text = rmd_lines[(start + 1):(end - 1)])
  this_run <- new.env()
  report_run <- new.env()
  report_run$mine <- report_tables
  capture.output(invisible(eval(slide_code, this_run)))
  capture.output(invisible(eval(slide_code, report_run)))

  # a cell differs if only one side is missing, or if both are there and differ
  ours <- cells(this_run$tables)
  theirs <- cells(report_run$tables)
  if (length(ours) != length(theirs)) {
    differ <- seq_along(ours)
  } else {
    missing_differs <- is.na(ours) != is.na(theirs)
    value_differs <- !is.na(ours) & !is.na(theirs) & ours != theirs
    differ <- which(missing_differs | value_differs)
  }
  if (length(differ) > 0) {
    details[[slide_id]] <- data.frame(
      slide = slide_id,
      this_file = ours[differ],
      report = theirs[differ][seq_along(differ)]
    )
  }

  # every number inside a cell counts, including years and counts
  numbers_in_cells <- regmatches(ours, gregexpr("[0-9][0-9,]*(\\.[0-9]+)?", ours))
  result <- rbind(result, data.frame(
    Slide = sub("slide-", "Slide ", slide_id),
    `Numbers compared` = sum(lengths(numbers_in_cells)),
    `Text cells compared` = sum(!grepl("[0-9]", ours)),
    Mismatches = length(differ),
    Result = if (length(differ) > 0) "FAIL" else "pass",
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
all_slides <- data.frame(
  Slide = "All slides",
  `Numbers compared` = sum(result$`Numbers compared`),
  `Text cells compared` = sum(result$`Text cells compared`),
  Mismatches = sum(result$Mismatches),
  Result = if (all(result$Result == "pass")) "pass" else "FAIL",
  check.names = FALSE
)
result <- rbind(result, all_slides)
cat("\n\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  result,
  caption = "Printed numbers: this file against the report's outputs", align = "lrrrl"
))
cat("\n\n")
if (length(details) > 0) {
  differences <- bind_rows(details)
  print(knitr::kable(differences, caption = "Cells that differ"))
  stop(
    "The numbers printed by this file differ from the report's outputs on ", length(details),
    " slide(s)."
  )
}
```
